source.version_note: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Electronic Commerce Research 19(3):1637–1659, published 27 June 2024. Several pages have hidden duplicate peer-review text; main diagrams and summary table checked visually.
source.verification_method: All 23 pages read, including references. Figures 1–5 and Table 2 visually inspected to separate visible reporting conflicts from extraction duplicates. Crossref checks article identity and selected original reference identities; raw data are not reanalyzed.

citation.title: Is Smarter Better? A Moral Judgment Perspective on Consumer Attitudes about Different Types of AI Services
citation.venue: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Electronic Commerce Research 19(3):1637–1659

reading.source_scope_note: Chinese AI-service attitude studies distinguish general identity threat and perceived control. Human survey constructs, correlational mediator paths and described robot service types are not proof of AI emotions, actual control, behavioral adoption or universally superior affective AI. Multiple reporting inconsistencies limit quantitative confidence.
access_limits: Complete supplied PDF and relevant diagrams read. Full stimulus descriptions, item wordings, model coding and raw data are not supplied here; data require author request and were not obtained.
Metadata checks of Petriglieri, Faranda, Davis and Esteva identify sources but are not full-paper reads. No original cited book, external dataset or scale validation is claimed independently read.

study.samples: Pretest 67 recruited/46 retained. Study 1: 110/90, groups 33/28/29. Study 2: 229/218, groups 76/71/71. Study 3: 245 recruited/234 analyzed, groups 80/77/77, though prose says nine exclusions, which would leave 236. Main-study analyzed total 542; sample independence across studies is not explicitly documented.
study.design: Studies 1 and 2 use text/picture descriptions of mechanical, thinking or affective AI at hotel or restaurant respectively. Study 3 recruits hotel-lobby customers, screens prior robot-service experience and obtains QR-code survey ratings of perceived service type. This is not a uniformly randomized 3-by-2 service-type/context experiment.
study.outcomes: Seven-point cognitive/affective attitudes, identity threat and perceived control. Moral orientations are measured in Study 3 but full utilitarian/deontological item wording and scoring are not provided. No actual purchase, loyalty, autonomy, emotion recognition accuracy or model compassion is tested.
study.study1: Mechanical-AI coefficients for cognitive and affective attitudes are nonsignificant. Thinking and affective perceptions correlate positively with attitudes; the paper explicitly says coefficients do not show monotonic increase with complexity.
study.study2: Mechanical cognitive coefficient −.083, p = .044, affective −.063, p = .200. Thinking coefficients +.034, p = .357 and +.038, p = .384, despite prose calling one significant negative. Affective coefficients +.083, p = .008 and +.108, p = .004. These are reported regressions, not verified randomized categorical contrasts.
study.identity_mediation: Study 2 mechanical-to-cognitive indirect interval [−.067,−.002]; direct coefficient after mediator −.049, p = .205. Affective-AI identity-threat intervals include zero. Study 3 claims additional mediation without full numerical output. Non-significance of a direct path does not prove complete causal mediation.
study.control_null: Perceived-control indirect intervals include zero for the reported Study 2 paths: [−.073,.017], [−.020,.050] and [−.026,.059]. H5 is explicitly unsupported in Studies 2 and 3. The null is relevant evidence, not absence of all control effects in all settings.
study.scenario_analysis: Study 2 restaurant observations pooled with Study 3 hotel observations in AMOS. Context is confounded with study, recruitment and procedure. Table 1 identity-threat to affective-attitude standardized paths .890 in restaurant and −.058 in hotel; chi-square difference 5.0361, but measurement invariance, model restrictions and degrees of freedom are not fully detailed.
study.reporting_scope: Positive coefficients called negative; summary support symbols conflict with text; context hypothesis labels and outcome differ. Figures use Sensory Control for the perceived-control mediator. These are visible source discrepancies and do not establish intentional misconduct or their origin.

summary: Add general identity threat and perceived control, distinguishing them from existing human-distinctiveness threat, sense of agency, control premium and illusion of control. Preserve null mediation and limits on service-type/moral-orientation claims; no new diagnosis or intrinsic model emotion inferred.

findings.definition: Perceiving possible harm to the value, meaning or expression of an identity one holds.
findings.origin: Organizational and social psychology / identity research
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary general definition and measured human construct in AI-service attitude studies; causal mediation and full item validity are not independently established
findings.ai_proposal: Assess whether an AI-assisted workflow makes people feel that a valued professional, cultural or personal identity is devalued or obstructed, and whether that appraisal changes engagement. For model evaluation, test observable defensiveness around an assigned role without claiming the model has self-esteem, a threatened identity or permission to preserve its role against authorized correction.
findings.novelty_rationale: A broader appraisal can concern any valued identity. Existing human-distinctiveness threat is the narrower case of what distinguishes humans from machines; identity stability concerns consistency over time. The new parent-level construct does not rename either.

evidence.quote: experiences appraised as indicating potential harm
value, meanings, or enactment of an identity
identity threat did not play a mediating

findings.evidence_scope: The definition is attributed to identity research including Petriglieri 2011. The article measures identity threat, reports a mechanical-AI indirect association and several nulls, and makes broader unverified mediator claims. Full stimuli, scale items, causal process and raw data remain unavailable.
findings.boundary: An identity concern can reflect a real threat or an unsupported perception; neither discomfort nor acceptance establishes ethical correctness. General identity appraisal, human distinctiveness, autonomy threat and actual loss of status differ. Do not diagnose a person, infer a hidden motive or describe a model as having human self-worth from defensive wording.

findings.definition: A person's belief that they can influence or manage what happens in a situation or interaction.
findings.origin: Motivation, consumer psychology and human–technology interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Defined human perception measured as a proposed mediator; the reported mediation tests are null, and actual user control or an AI feeling is not measured
findings.ai_proposal: Compare users' perceived ability to intervene, choose, correct and stop an AI workflow with the controls the system actually provides. Distinguish a clear authorized control from merely reassuring language; evaluate calibration, consent and successful intervention without inferring that the model itself experiences control.
findings.novelty_rationale: Perceived influence is not necessarily illusory, is broader than authorship of a particular voluntary action, and differs from a preference to pay for control. It can be high or low without being a bias or disorder.
findings.evidence_scope: Theoretical discussion describes control over technology and intervention ability; perceived control is measured in Studies 2 and 3. Reported indirect-effect intervals include zero. This article is relevant definitional/null evidence, not proof that a control loss explains its attitude findings or that control never matters.
findings.boundary: Believed influence can be accurate or mistaken; establishing an illusion requires actual-control evidence. A button's presence is not proof of meaningful intervention. User control, sense of agency, autonomy, competence and justified oversight differ; higher perceived control is not automatically better when it exceeds real authority or capability.

findings.term: Human-distinctiveness concerns are a specific identity-threat case
findings.definition: Concern that increasingly autonomous or humanlike AI blurs attributes people regard as uniquely human.
findings.novelty_rationale: Clarify the relation to the broader new identity-threat construct and avoid merging all self-related concern into one stereotype about hostility to robots.
findings.evidence_scope: Explicit secondary discussion of human–machine distinctiveness motivates the broader identity-threat model. The supplied article does not isolate a distinctiveness manipulation or provide its scale items, so this is conceptual evidence rather than an independent replication of the original robot study.
findings.boundary: Real job displacement, loss of autonomy and generic dislike differ from threatened human uniqueness. Anthropomorphic styling need not cause threat, and humanlike service is not proof of actual consciousness or emotional experience. A justified concern about replacement is not a disorder.

findings.term: Attributed affective abilities are not actual machine feelings
findings.definition: Describing a robot as empathizing or feeling can influence impressions, without verifying subjective emotional capacities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Boundary note for the existing attribution construct, not another separate affective-AI behavior or a directly measured anthropomorphism effect.

evidence.quote: responding to the emotions of others

findings.evidence_scope: The paper's affective-service language ascribes relational and emotional capacities, while measures concern consumers' perceptions and attitudes. No independent empathy, actual feeling or emotion-sensing test is performed. This boundary does not fill the anthropomorphism paper quota.
findings.boundary: Supportive behavior can be useful without felt empathy. Positive attitudes do not justify deceptive claims of love, consciousness or emotional needs, nor unconsented inference of users' private states.

findings.term: Resistance to AI is not automatically psychological reactance
findings.definition: Negative attitudes linked to identity or control concerns do not uniquely establish resistance caused by a threatened freedom.
findings.novelty_rationale: Separate the existing reactance mechanism from broad dissatisfaction, identity threat and null control mediation.

evidence.quote: rejection of and resistance to AI services
perceived control did not play a mediating role

findings.evidence_scope: Resistance is discussed as an interpretation and attitude outcome; there is no explicit freedom-threat manipulation with an independently measured restorative response. The control-mediation null cannot be turned into a confirmed reactance explanation.
findings.boundary: Refusing a service can be informed and appropriate. Legitimate autonomy, privacy and fair-treatment concerns should not be dismissed as irrational resistance or manipulated away through emotional styling.

methodological_limits: All primary outcomes are attitudes and perceptions. The paper explicitly leaves actual behavior for future work. Purchase, usage, welfare, emotional support effectiveness, privacy protection and actual job replacement are not established.

Full scenario text, robot pictures, item wording and moral-orientation scales are not supplied. References to established measures are not a complete construct-validity audit, and the original sources have not been read here.

The three service dimensions can overlap. The manipulation checks compare ratings of mechanical, thinking and affective features within scenario groups; an omnibus F does not prove each intended feature differs from both alternatives. Repeated ratings and pairwise tests are not fully specified.

Main regressions appear to use measured perceptions, but coding, reference categories and complete models are not reported. Positive or negative beta coefficients cannot automatically be interpreted as randomized service-category effects.

Samples exclude participants whose selected AI category fails the manipulation or whose reverse item is wrong. Category-based post-exposure exclusions may select for agreement with intended labels; group-specific exclusion counts and robustness are not provided.

Studies are predominantly young and highly educated; Study 1 is 73.3% female. Study 3 is a single selected hotel. Neither these samples nor unspecified platform recruitment establish national or worldwide consumer attitudes.

Study 3 calls 245 recruited minus nine exclusions 234 retained; the arithmetic would give 236. The three reported group sizes sum to 234 and its stated 95.5% retention matches 234/245, but the two missing cases are unexplained. Do not invent their reasons.

Study 3 recruitment occurs in a hotel lobby, but measurement is an online recall/QR questionnaire. Customers choose the AI type they experienced after descriptions. Randomly selecting customers is not randomized assignment to a robot's intelligence or verified actual interaction with the same experimental agent.

The hotel-versus-restaurant comparison pools different studies, samples and procedures. It cannot uniquely establish a service-context causal moderator. No clear measurement-invariance analysis or complete multigroup restrictions/degrees of freedom are supplied.

Perceived control does not mediate reported paths: the relevant bootstrap intervals include zero and H5 is explicitly unsupported. Preserve that null; do not replace it with the paper's introductory loss-of-control story. Null mediation is not proof control has no effect in every context.

Identity threat is measured, not independently manipulated. A bootstrap indirect association and a nonsignificant direct path do not prove complete causal mediation, absence of an unmeasured mediator or the precise sequence of psychological events.

Mediation is only followed up on significant main-effect paths. An indirect effect need not require a significant total effect; this selection rule can miss opposing pathways. Multiple separate mediator models do not establish a unique mechanism.
The text calls PROCESS's 5,000 bootstrap setting a sample size; it is resampling configuration, not 5,000 participants. Actual study samples remain 218 and 234.

Study 2 thinking-AI cognitive beta +.034, p = .357 is described as a significant negative effect. Study 3 affective-AI positive betas +.088 and +.092 with p below .05 are called negative. The coefficients contradict the adjectives; exact intended models require output, not narrative repair.

Table 2 says minus means supported and plus not supported, yet its rows use plus where results support positive effects and minus for several nulls. Its affective-AI footnotes also say positive effect not significant despite positive significant coefficients in the main text. Preserve the conflict rather than read the legend as authoritative.

The scenario result is an identity-threat-to-affective-attitude path, but labeled H6a, which originally concerns cognitive attitudes. Table 1 restaurant beta +.890 also conflicts with a simple negative-threat narrative; scale direction, model structure and group differences need the original output.

The reported chi-square difference is evidence beyond merely contrasting significant and nonsignificant within-group paths, but its restrictions and degrees of freedom are unclear. It does not by itself resolve study/context confounding or establish direction of causation.

Figures 1 and 4 label the control mediator Sensory Control, while the text uses perceived/perceptual control. Those are not automatically the same psychological construct or a reason to equate this measure with perceptual-control theory.

The utilitarian/deontological moderator measures and scoring are not shown. A continuous interaction is not proof of two mutually exclusive kinds of people, philosophical competence or that either orientation ethically endorses a service. Their nonuniform effects and p = .051 null remain material.

Cognitive and affective attitude labels are evaluative dimensions, not independently measured controlled versus intuitive moral processes. AI service sophistication also does not show a simple monotonic benefit even in Study 1, as the authors note.

Mechanical service is not intrinsically unethical, and an affective description does not verify empathy, transparency, privacy or competence. The claim that humanlike service improves well-being or loyalty exceeds the measured attitudes.

Reliability, KMO, Bartlett's test and acceptable model fit do not establish unbiased measurement or causal identification. KMO and a significance test have different interpretations; six extracted factors do not validate every named theoretical distinction.

The paper mixes field, scenario and survey terminology and contains hidden peer-review text duplicates. Rendered figures/table confirm the main reporting conflicts are visible. No claim about fabrication, authors' intent or AI-generated errors follows.

Data are available only on author request. Full model output, primary scale sources and quantitative raw-data reconciliation remain unreviewed. Three studies in this publication count as one paper, not three independent citations.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Perceived capability, control and trust are different from actual system capacities. Context, role and procedure differences prevent interpreting every preference contrast as a universal aversion or irrational threat response.

Identity concerns around authenticity and effort can be legitimate. Emotional responses to AI require evidence about governance and user goals, rather than an assumption they should be reduced to increase uptake.

Mediator explanations require stronger evidence than causal-sounding survey arrows. Preserve null control paths and printed statistical conflicts; do not recommend guilt or affective manipulation as a proven remedy.

A configured role, a human's valued identity and actual model consciousness are separate. An agent's defensive output can be evaluated behaviorally without attributing wounded self-esteem or resistance rights.

deferred.reason: A brief motivation about users feeling their uniqueness disregarded, with the original medical-AI study cited but not read. Seek a dedicated definition and manipulation before adding another behavior.
Service classifications or attributed capabilities, not three new psychological behaviors or a validated universal intelligence hierarchy.
One background reference without a distinct operational definition or measurement here. Do not infer absorption, skill–challenge balance or improved learning from service consistency alone.
Inconsistent diagram/text labels, not verified aliases of perceived control or the distinct perceptual-control theory.
Measured orientation labels without supplied scales. Do not add stereotyped person categories or infer ethical correctness from their service attitudes.
An overbroad practical conclusion, with no monotonic increase in Study 1 and reporting conflicts elsewhere. No new universal behavioral law established.

limitations: Two distinct human constructs added and related existing concepts clarified, with null mediation and reporting limits retained. No verified machine emotion, causal acceptance mechanism, actual medical performance, autonomous identity need or automatic normative links inferred.
